title: Education stocks: how to analyze education companies
description: Education stocks are paid per pupil, not per business cycle. How to read pupil volumes, funding models and supervision risk — AcadeMedia worked through.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Education stocks are shares in companies that deliver education as a service: running preschools and schools on public funding, selling examinations and digital learning materials, or operating education providers against tuition fees. The sector's analytical profile fits in one sentence: revenues are paid per pupil, per examination or per delivered service — not per business cycle. AcadeMedia, Sweden's largest education company, reported net revenue of SEK 20,360 million (+7.0 percent) for the financial year 2025/26 and an operating profit of SEK 1,947 million, with an average of 115,270 children and pupils in preschool, compulsory and upper secondary school.

This guide walks through the three business models, the mechanics of per-pupil funding, the arithmetic of volume, price and margin — and what supervision and the residency requirement mean for risk. AcadeMedia runs as the worked example, with Pearson, Laureate Education and Grand Canyon Education as comparators.

## Three business models — what education stocks earn money on

**Operating per pupil.** AcadeMedia is organized into four segments — preschools, compulsory schools, upper secondary schools and adult education — with operations outside Sweden mainly in Norway and Germany. Revenue is public funding per child and pupil, complemented by competitively tendered adult education — municipalities and authorities procure training places, giving contract-bound volumes at set prices. Operating margins sit around nine to twelve percent: capital requirements are low but payroll is large — staff the biggest cost item and the most important quality carrier — and the price of the core service is politically set.

**Services and licenses.** Pearson has left its publishing years behind and sells examinations, English-language teaching, digital materials and workforce skills. Full year 2025: sales of £3,577 million (+4 percent on an underlying basis) and an adjusted operating margin of 17.2 percent, up from 16.9. Margins run higher than in school operations, at the price of customers with budget cycles of their own.

**Tuition fees.** Laureate Education operates private universities mainly in Mexico and Peru; revenue in 2025 was 1.702 billion dollars, up 8.6 percent, and in the first quarter of 2026 it grew a further 15 percent to 272.6 million dollars. Here the payer is the household, often through student loans — demand follows the labor market and the credit system, not birth rates.

An intermediate form is Grand Canyon Education: the company carries a university's digital operations, marketing and support for around 60 percent of its revenue — an OPM model, online program management — with service revenue around 1.1 billion dollars in 2025. Three models, three payers: the municipality, the institution, the household.

## Per-pupil funding — the mechanism that carries the revenues

The legal name is grant to independent school operators (in Swedish: bidrag till enskilda huvudmän). The home municipality pays the independent school an amount per pupil, in line with its own average cost per pupil — premises costs included — normally monthly. Three consequences follow directly from the construction.

First: volume is the pupil count — more children is more revenue, because the funding follows the pupil. Second: the price is the municipality's cost level, not the company's bargaining strength — revenue per pupil follows municipal cost decisions. Third: demand is demographic, not cyclical. The preschool intake follows the number of children born, with a few years' lag; adult education grows in downturns, when unemployed people are retrained. As a whole, the sector's revenues are more stable than cyclical industries' — the theme in [revenue stability](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys) — but with a political risk premium as the price.

## AcadeMedia worked through — volume, price and margin

Two financial years put the mechanism on the table. 2024/25: net revenue SEK 19,021 million, operating profit SEK 1,752 million — a margin of 9.2 percent. 2025/26: SEK 20,360 million (+7.0 percent), operating profit SEK 1,947 million (+11.1 percent) — a margin of 9.6 percent. The average pupil count rose from 111,290 to 115,270 — 3.6 percent.

Decompose the growth: 7.0 percent at 3.6 percent volume growth gives a price and mix effect of around 3.3 percent (1.070 divided by 1.036). The calculation separates organic from acquired growth and shows which engine carries. A rough coverage check: SEK 20,360 million divided by 115,270 children and pupils gives roughly SEK 177,000 in revenue per place — a number to follow over time and across segments, noting that adult education and international operations add revenue without appearing in the pupil count.

Then leverage. A preschool department with 50 places and 40 children has fixed costs — premises, staff — that do not grow with the last five children. Fill five places and volume rises 12.5 percent on a practically unchanged cost base. That is why occupancy shows up directly in the margin. AcadeMedia's fourth quarter (April–June, the spring term's end) 2025/26 posted revenue of SEK 5,658 million (+10.6 percent) with an operating margin of 11.8 percent, and the pupil count that quarter was 119,430, up 5.2 percent. The seasonal pattern means the [quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) must be read against the calendar, not quarter against quarter unadjusted.

## Regulation — permits, supervision and the residency requirement

Education is heavily regulated, and regulation is the sector's primary source of risk. The Swedish Schools Inspectorate examines permits for new establishments and expansions, exercises ongoing supervision and can, in serious cases, prohibit an operator from admitting new pupils. Since 1 August 2022 a residency requirement also applies: an independent school may only admit a pupil if the pupil or guardian is resident in Sweden or another EEA country, and profit distribution in school-essential operations requires permission. Politics keeps moving — the inquiry Skärpta villkor för friskolesektorn (Tighter conditions for the independent school sector, SOU 2025:37) was delivered in 2025 — so the pace of change in the rules of the game is never zero. The equivalents among the comparators: Pearson's dependence on examination regulation, Grand Canyon's on the American student loan system. [Regulatory risk](/kurser/rk-06-regulatorisk-risk) works through the assessments variable by variable.

## The key ratios — a checklist in four families

- **Volume.** Pupil count, split into organic and acquired growth; occupancy per operation. AcadeMedia reports average numbers per quarter — read the series, not individual quarters.
- **Price.** Funding per pupil, index uplifts, currency exposure in international operations.
- **Profitability and cash flow.** Operating margin per segment, revenue per pupil and the payroll share — together with [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen), since grants are paid in arrears and working capital swings with term starts.
- **Valuation.** The multiple against the company's own history; stable revenues and political risk pull in opposite directions, and [the P/E ratio](/kurser/km-009-pe) becomes meaningful only against the sector's normal level.

## Three risks specific to education stocks

- **The political one.** Funding levels, residency requirements and inquiries — the revenue formula can be rewritten by legislation.
- **The demographic one.** Shrinking cohorts mean a lower intake a few years later; growth must then be carried by adult education, international operations or acquisitions.
- **The quality-bearing one.** Supervision reviews, grade debates and individual incidents strike directly at reputation — the customer is the guardian, the payer the municipality.

## The summary

- Three business models: operating per pupil (AcadeMedia), services and licenses (Pearson), tuition fees (Laureate) — with the OPM model (Grand Canyon Education) as intermediate form.
- Per-pupil funding: volume is the pupil count, price is the municipality's cost level, demand is set by demographics.
- AcadeMedia 2025/26: revenue +7.0 percent = volume +3.6 multiplied by price and mix +3.3; operating margin from 9.2 to 9.6 percent, with the spring term higher.
- Regulation is risk number one: permits, supervision, the residency requirement and an ongoing inquiry.
